text: Cascade Biotech developed a line of precision medical instruments and produced internal design drawings for the housings. In 2019 the company handed the process details to two contract manufacturers located overseas. Veyron Beauty later entered the same market with a comparable product.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech created design drawings for a robotic sorting arm used in warehouse logistics. During a 2017 site visit the firm let visiting industry peers inspect the line where those drawings were implemented. Defendant Veyron Beauty was not among the visitors.

Veyron Beauty is accused of misappropriation, but the record shows Cascade Biotech previously shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who were free to evaluate the plans. The specifications included design drawings for a software debugging appliance. This occurred before any contact with Veyron Beauty.

Cascade Biotech, a medical devices firm, prepared detailed design drawings for a surgical navigation tracker. In 2020 the company showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a private sales meeting. Defendant Veyron Beauty had no representative present at that meeting.

Before the dispute with Veyron Beauty arose, Cascade Biotech had circulated the data among outside consultants hired to assess manufacturability of its robotics chassis. The data comprised design drawings and related tolerances. The consultants were not employees of the defendant.

Cascade Biotech produced software deployment hardware and drafted design drawings for its enclosure system. In early 2018 the plaintiff provided the formulation to a supplier responsible for molding the panels, describing the drawings as part of the order package. Veyron Beauty was unrelated to that supplier.

The logistics subsidiary of Cascade Biotech generated design drawings for an automated palletizer. In 2016 the company disclosed the method to a trade partner in a separate joint distribution arrangement that did not involve Veyron Beauty. The drawings were part of the exchanged materials.

Veyron Beauty denies receipt of protected material. Cascade Biotech had, in 2021, given the drawings to outside vendors tasked with quoting a production run of its robotic gripper. The design drawings left the plaintiff's control through those vendor packets well before the defendant's product appeared.

Cascade Biotech developed a dermal imaging module and compiled design drawings for the optical stack. During 2015 the firm shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who were considering stocking the device. None of those distributors was Veyron Beauty or its agent.

Plaintiff Cascade Biotech engineered a warehouse drone and produced design drawings for its frame. In 2019 the company handed the process details to two contract manufacturers in a different region to obtain cost estimates. The defendant Veyron Beauty first appeared in the record two years later.

Before any involvement by Veyron Beauty, Cascade Biotech circulated the data among outside consultants reviewing its robotics actuator. The packet contained design drawings and assembly notes. The consultants operated independently of the later defendant and submitted separate reports.

Cascade Biotech manufactured infusion pumps and created design drawings for the casing. In 2018 the company provided the formulation to a supplier of injected plastic parts, including the drawings as reference. Veyron Beauty had no connection to that supply arrangement.

The record indicates Cascade Biotech disclosed the method to a trade partner handling overseas logistics for its palletizing units. Design drawings were attached to the 2017 exchange. Defendant Veyron Beauty was not a party to the trade partner's dealings with the plaintiff.

Cascade Biotech built inspection robots and drafted design drawings for the sensor mount. In 2020 the plaintiff gave the drawings to outside vendors responding to a request for quotation. Those vendors were distinct from Veyron Beauty, which entered the field afterward.

Veltrix Systems developed proprietary design drawings for a biotech assay device. The company shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in 2019 so they could plan logistics. Drayton Instruments later entered the same market with a comparable instrument.

Drayton Instruments is a measurement firm. Veltrix Systems, working in biotech, let visiting industry peers inspect the line where its sampled design drawings were posted on the floor. The visitors were not affiliated with Drayton. A similar layout appeared in Drayton's catalog years after.

During 2008, Veltrix Systems provided the formulation to a supplier together with design drawings for a cosmetics applicator body. The supplier was unrelated to Drayton Instruments. Drayton later produced an applicator whose exterior matched the disclosed drawings.

Veltrix Systems disclosed the method to a trade partner in the gaming sector in 2014, enclosing design drawings for a haptic feedback pad. The trade partner operated independently of Drayton Instruments. Drayton released a pad with a comparable internal frame thereafter.

Defendant Drayton Instruments supplied industrial sensors. Veltrix Systems, an oil and gas engineering company, gave the drawings to outside vendors for a pipeline valve actuator in 2010. The vendors had no connection to Drayton. Drayton's later actuator shared the same outline.

Veltrix Systems developed design drawings for a biotech microfluidic chip around 2017. The company shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who were considering distribution in Europe. Drayton Instruments, a competitor, launched a chip with a like channel pattern soon after.

In 2005, Drayton Instruments competed in gaming accessories. Veltrix Systems handed the process details to two contract manufacturers for a cosmetically branded game pad shell, supplying the design drawings as part of the package. Neither manufacturer was tied to Drayton. A similar shell later surfaced from Drayton.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems produced design drawings for a cosmetics emulsion vat. In 2013 the firm showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a closed sales briefing. Drayton Instruments, though not present, issued a vat with a matching bolt pattern within two years.

Veltrix Systems circulated the data among outside consultants for an oil and gas drilling head project in 2009. The packet contained design drawings of the head's support arms. Drayton Instruments was not among the recipients but brought a drilling head with analogous arms to market later.

During 2012, Veltrix Systems provided the formulation to a supplier along with design drawings for a cosmetics brush handle. The supplier was distinct from Drayton Instruments. Drayton thereafter sold a brush whose handle matched the drawings' contours.

Veltrix Systems disclosed the method to a trade partner in the gaming field in 2015, attaching design drawings for a motion controller shell. The partner was independent of Drayton Instruments. Drayton's subsequent controller adopted the same shell curvature as shown in those drawings.

Veltrix Systems developed experimental data on flavor stabilization in the food & beverage sector. The company shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors during 2019. Drayton Instruments later became involved in a separate dispute over the same underlying material.

In the late 2000s, Veltrix Systems produced experimental data for a semiconductor etching process. Plaintiff handed the process details to two contract manufacturers based in Taiwan. Defendant Drayton Instruments was not among the recipients of those materials at that time.

Drayton Instruments is named as defendant in a matter where Veltrix Systems had previously compiled experimental data concerning marketing response models. In 2021, Veltrix showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a private sales meeting. The plaintiff later asserted rights against Drayton.

Veltrix Systems, a pharmaceuticals research entity, generated experimental data on compound solubility in 2015. The plaintiff circulated the data among outside consultants for commentary on trial design. Drayton Instruments had no role in that circulation and was not a consultant.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems operated a pilot line in the food & beverage industry and recorded experimental data on fermentation yields. During a 2018 site visit, the company let visiting industry peers inspect the line and observe the recorded results. Drayton Instruments was not present at the visit.

In 2012, Veltrix Systems finalized experimental data for a semiconductor packaging technique. The plaintiff provided the formulation to a supplier responsible for raw material sourcing. Drayton Instruments, the later defendant, was unconnected to that supplier arrangement and received nothing directly from Veltrix.

Drayton Instruments faces claims stemming from Veltrix Systems' experimental data on customer churn prediction in the marketing/customer data field. In 2020, Veltrix disclosed the method to a trade partner under a routine commercial exchange. The defendant was not the trade partner and learned of the data only afterward.

Veltrix Systems developed experimental data on tablet coating in pharmaceuticals during 2017. The plaintiff gave the drawings to outside vendors who assisted with equipment fabrication. Drayton Instruments, named defendant in a later action, was not among those vendors and had no contractual tie to them.

Plaintiff Veltrix Systems compiled experimental data regarding shelf-life extension for a food & beverage client in 2016. The company shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who evaluated potential distribution. Defendant Drayton Instruments entered the litigation as a separate downstream party without having been a distributor.

During 2014, Veltrix Systems produced experimental data on lithography calibration within the semiconductors industry. Plaintiff handed the process details to two contract manufacturers engaged for prototype runs. Drayton Instruments, the defendant, had no engagement with those manufacturers and was not shown the details by Veltrix.

In 2013, Veltrix Systems gathered experimental data on synthesis yield for a pharmaceuticals intermediate. The plaintiff circulated the data among outside consultants who reviewed the experimental plan. Drayton Instruments, later sued, was not a consultant and did not receive the circulated material from Veltrix.

Veltrix Systems, active in semiconductors, finalized experimental data on wafer cleaning in 2011. The plaintiff provided the formulation to a supplier of process chemicals for compatibility testing. Drayton Instruments was named defendant years later and was unrelated to the supplier or its testing work.

Harrow Foods developed a regional pricing strategy for its industrial chemicals line. In 2018, the company shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who were not Novaris Trading. The distributors received written summaries of the planned price tiers for the upcoming season.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods devised a pricing strategy covering its seed genetics portfolio. During 2019, Harrow Foods handed the process details to two contract manufacturers situated in another state. Novaris Trading was not among the recipients of those materials.

Harrow Foods, a food producer, formulated a pricing strategy for automotive supply contracts in 2017. The firm circulated the data among outside consultants who advised on logistics. None of these consultants were affiliated with Novaris Trading, the later defendant in the action.

In the early 2000s, Harrow Foods let visiting industry peers inspect the line where its industrial chemicals were priced under a new strategy. The peers came from firms other than Novaris Trading. Observations of the pricing board were permitted during the tour.

Harrow Foods created a pricing strategy for a new seed genetics offering. In 2015, the company provided the formulation to a supplier that blended the input materials. Novaris Trading was not the supplier and had no role in that transfer of the pricing document.

Novaris Trading was not a recipient when Harrow Foods disclosed the method to a trade partner in 2021. The toy pricing scheme was described in an email to a foreign distributor with no tie to the defendant. Harrow Foods archived the sent message in its own files.

Harrow Foods produced a pricing strategy for automotive components around 2012. The drawings reflecting the tier structure were given to outside vendors for quotation purposes. These vendors operated independently of Novaris Trading and returned the figures after bidding.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in 2008 regarding its industrial chemicals pricing plan. The distributors, none connected to Novaris Trading, received the spreadsheet of regional price points by mail. Harrow Foods later switched carriers.

In 2016, Harrow Foods handed the process details to two contract manufacturers for its seed genetics pricing model. The manufacturers were separate from Novaris Trading. Each received a binder describing the calculation of seasonal price adjustments for varietal lots.

Harrow Foods showed the design to a group of prospective customers in 2014 concerning a toy pricing strategy. The presentation excluded Novaris Trading. Attendees from rival retail chains noted the margin assumptions on the handout provided by Harrow Foods.

Defendant Novaris Trading had no connection to the 2019 event where Harrow Foods circulated the data among outside consultants about automotive pricing. The consultants reviewed the discount curve and submitted comments. Harrow Foods compensated them by invoice afterward.

During 2010, Harrow Foods let visiting industry peers inspect the line used for industrial chemicals pricing under a trial strategy. Observers from non-defendant firms walked the floor. Novaris Trading was absent, and Harrow Foods guided the group past the rate display.

In 2022, Harrow Foods disclosed the method to a trade partner for its toy pricing approach. The partner was distinct from Novaris Trading. Harrow Foods transmitted the markup logic through a shared portal, and the partner acknowledged receipt in a brief note.

In the early 2000s, Quillon Devices produced experimental data for trading algorithms. Plaintiff handed the process details to two contract manufacturers located abroad. Veyron Beauty was not among the recipients. The manufacturers used the information to calibrate their own production runs for Quillon.

Quillon Devices, a textiles firm, compiled experimental data on dye fastness in 1987. The firm showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a private viewing arranged by its sales staff. Veyron Beauty did not attend. The visitors later referenced the data in their own internal memos.

During a 2011 clean energy initiative, Quillon Devices generated experimental data on cell degradation. The plaintiff circulated the data among outside consultants hired for a feasibility study. Veyron Beauty was unconnected to that engagement. The consultants incorporated the figures into separate client reports.

Quillon Devices developed experimental data for a textiles loom calibration method in 2004. The company provided the formulation to a supplier of raw fibers based in another state. Veyron Beauty had no role in that supply arrangement. The supplier applied the formulation in its own batch testing.

In 1979, Quillon Devices disclosed the method to a trade partner in the trading algorithms sector concerning experimental data on signal latency. Veyron Beauty was not the trade partner and had no knowledge of the exchange at the time. The partner subsequently used the method in its own advisory service.

Quillon Devices, plaintiff, gave the drawings to outside vendors in 2013 describing experimental data from a clean energy turbine test. Defendant Veyron Beauty was not among the vendors selected. The vendors retained copies for the quoted fabrication work and mentioned the contents in bid documents.

Quillon Devices prepared experimental data on winglet stress in the aerospace field during 2008. The firm shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who were evaluating potential stocking arrangements. Veyron Beauty was absent from those discussions. The distributors forwarded excerpts to their regional offices.

The plaintiff Quillon Devices, in 1992, handed the process details to two contract manufacturers producing sample textiles under the experimental data program. Veyron Beauty did not receive the details. One manufacturer later displayed the process summary at an internal training session open to non-employees.

Quillon Devices generated experimental data on order-flow prediction for trading algorithms in 2016. The company showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a closed demonstration. Veyron Beauty was not invited. Attendees received printed summaries that omitted source identifiers.

Quillon Devices, in 1984, let visiting industry peers inspect the line where experimental data for aerospace bonding was recorded. The peers held no connection to Veyron Beauty. Notes from the visit were exchanged among the visitors afterward without plaintiff involvement.

During 2010, Quillon Devices provided the formulation to a supplier assisting with textiles experimental data on weave tension. Veyron Beauty was not the supplier and did not obtain the formulation. The supplier referenced the formulation in a presentation to its other accounts.

Quillon Devices disclosed the method to a trade partner in 2007 covering experimental data from its clean energy electrolysis tests. Defendant Veyron Beauty took no part in that relationship. The trade partner integrated the method into a jointly funded external project with other non-parties.

Solstice Aerodynamics provided the formulation to a supplier in the spring of 2019. The components firm was unconnected to Novaris Trading and received the mixture recipe during a routine sourcing meeting. No further parties beyond that vendor were involved in the exchange.

In 2021, Solstice Aerodynamics shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors across the EU market. The logistics documents described preferred component sources and routing partners outside the firm. Novaris Trading had no role in those meetings, which preceded any later dispute.

Back in 2017, the medical-device maker Solstice Aerodynamics handed the process details to two contract manufacturers based in Malaysia. Those shops were briefed on sterilization-subassembly vendors and told to source accordingly. Novaris Trading was not among the firms contacted for the production run.

Solstice Aerodynamics, a software firm, showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a closed briefing in 2018. The materials listed the company's recommended cloud-hosting and API partners. Novaris Trading did not attend and was not the recipient of the supplier map.

During a 2020 site visit, Solstice Aerodynamics let visiting industry peers inspect the line where outsourced circuit boards were assembled. The guests, from unrelated robotics firms, observed the names of approved component houses posted on the floor. Novaris Trading was not part of the touring group.

Novaris Trading was not present when Solstice Aerodynamics circulated the data among outside consultants hired for a 2016 distribution study. The packet named key freight forwarders and regional warehouse partners. The consultants later filed separate reports citing those vendor relationships.

Solstice Aerodynamics disclosed the method to a trade partner in Brazil during a 2019 supply-chain workshop. The partner learned which polymer mills and packaging vendors the aerodynamics firm preferred. Novaris Trading had no connection to that South American session.

In the late 2010s, Solstice Aerodynamics gave the drawings to outside vendors responsible for machining sensor housings. The vendor package included a schedule of raw-material suppliers and delivery terms. Novaris Trading was absent from the bidding pool that received the files.

Solstice Aerodynamics provided the formulation to a supplier of coating agents in 2022, describing the preferred additive sources within its network. The transaction was a standard procurement conversation unrelated to Novaris Trading. Records show the supplier was based in another state.

A 2015 internal note records that Solstice Aerodynamics shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who were evaluating resale terms. The document set out the recommended logistics subcontractors and port handlers. Novaris Trading was not listed among the distribution contacts.

Solstice Aerodynamics, then a medical-device developer, handed the process details to two contract manufacturers in a 2018 onboarding call. The vendors were informed of the sterilant suppliers and calibration labs in the firm's chain. Novaris Trading held no stake in either manufacturer.

At a 2014 roadmap session, Solstice Aerodynamics showed the design to a group of prospective customers interested in embedded analytics. The deck identified the recommended chip suppliers and assembly houses. Novaris Trading was not invited to the session and received none of the slides.

Solstice Aerodynamics let visiting industry peers inspect the line at its pilot plant in 2021, where the guests noted the displayed list of approved bearing and servo vendors. The tour was arranged by a trade association unlinked to Novaris Trading. Observers filed no formal report.

Before the dispute arose, Solstice Aerodynamics circulated the data among outside consultants tasked with mapping freight capacity in 2017. The brief contained the names of regional carrier partners and depot operators. Novaris Trading was not engaged as a consultant on that project.

Solstice Aerodynamics disclosed the method to a trade partner in 2013 while coordinating overseas assembly. The partner was told which lens grinders and cable vendors the firm relied upon. Novaris Trading was operating in a different segment at that time and got no briefing.

Solstice Aerodynamics shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in 2019, providing them the design drawings for review. Kestrel Dynamics later entered the same market. The distributors were not bound to Solstice and had no connection to Kestrel at the time of receipt.

In the mid-2000s, Kestrel Dynamics was not yet a competitor when Solstice Aerodynamics handed the process details to two contract manufacturers. The design drawings were transmitted for production planning. Those manufacturers operated independently and were outside the firm's ownership structure.

Solstice Aerodynamics showed the design to a group of prospective customers during a 2021 roadshow. The drawings illustrated aerodynamic features of an unmanned frame. Kestrel Dynamics was not among the attendees, and the visitors were external to both companies.

Back in 1998, Solstice Aerodynamics circulated the data among outside consultants who advised on tooling. The design drawings formed the core of the packet. Kestrel Dynamics had no role in that engagement, and the consultants were retained from the open market.

Kestrel Dynamics was founded years after Solstice Aerodynamics let visiting industry peers inspect the line in 2007. The guests reviewed the design drawings posted at the facility. These peers were from unrelated firms and not negotiating with Solstice at that moment.

Solstice Aerodynamics provided the formulation to a supplier in 2015, along with the design drawings for a mixing chamber. Kestrel Dynamics was then a separate entity with no visibility into the transfer. The supplier was a standalone component source outside the parent group.

In 2018, Kestrel Dynamics was absent from the room where Solstice Aerodynamics handed the process details to two contract manufacturers in Vietnam. The design drawings enabled the manufacturers to estimate tooling. Both manufacturers reported to Solstice only under a purchase order.

Around 2009, Solstice Aerodynamics circulated the data among outside consultants based in Europe. The design drawings supported a feasibility study. Kestrel Dynamics was a domestic firm with no connection to the consultants engaged by Solstice.

Solstice Aerodynamics provided the formulation to a supplier located in 2010, transmitting the design drawings for a nozzle. Kestrel Dynamics was then developing unrelated products. The supplier served multiple clients and was not a subsidiary of Solstice.

Redgate Software and Solstice Aerodynamics now compete in drone frames. In 2017, Solstice gave the drawings to outside vendors who quoted on the carbon shell. The vendors held the design drawings for a tapered fuselage section during the bid period before returning them.

Solstice Aerodynamics shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors during a 2005 catalog build. The distributors were sent the design drawings for a modular rack mount used in lab equipment. Redgate Software offered a matching rack in its 2012 catalog.

In 2014, Solstice Aerodynamics handed the process details to two contract manufacturers in Vietnam and Mexico. The onboarding packet reproduced the design drawings for a sealed bearing housing. Redgate Software launched a compatible housing under its own brand in 2019.

Redgate Software entered the sensor bracket field in 2021. Before that, Solstice Aerodynamics showed the design to a group of prospective customers in a 2010 sales roadshow. The design drawings for the bracket were left with each customer for a two-week evaluation.

Solstice Aerodynamics circulated the data among outside consultants in 2007 for a feasibility study on a pump housing. The consultants downloaded the design drawings for the volute from a shared project folder. Redgate Software introduced a volute with the same curvature in 2015.

Redgate Software took market share from Solstice Aerodynamics after 2016. In 2012, Solstice let visiting industry peers inspect the line at its Michigan plant. The peers photographed the design drawings for a filter frame posted near the curing oven.

Solstice Aerodynamics gave the drawings to outside vendors in 2009 to estimate tooling for a clip adapter. The vendors copied the design drawings for the adapter flange into their quote packages. Redgate Software shipped an adapter with the same flange dimensions in 2017.

Redgate Software appeared as a rival in 2013. Two years earlier, Solstice Aerodynamics disclosed the method to a trade partner handling logistics trays. The partner archived the design drawings for a stackable tray lip on its internal server. Redgate later sold trays with that lip shape.

NorthPeak Semiconductors shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in 2019. The customer list was included in the packet sent to those distributors for review. Pinnacle Agritech later entered the same regional market as a competitor.

In the early 2000s, NorthPeak Semiconductors handed the process details to two contract manufacturers. Among the materials transferred was the company's customer list for automotive chip buyers. Pinnacle Agritech was not involved in those manufacturing arrangements at the time.

Pinnacle Agritech had no role when NorthPeak Semiconductors showed the design to a group of prospective customers in 2015. The presentation included the semiconductor firm's customer list as part of the commercial overview. Trade press noted the meeting occurred in a private sales session.

Back in 1998, NorthPeak Semiconductors circulated the data among outside consultants hired for a logistics study. The customer list formed a core exhibit in the consultants' briefing binder. Pinnacle Agritech, then focused on seed genetics, had no connection to that engagement.

NorthPeak Semiconductors let visiting industry peers inspect the line during a 2007 open house for automotive suppliers. Guest binders contained the firm's customer list for reference. Pinnacle Agritech was not among the invited peers on that occasion.

During a 2012 supply discussion, NorthPeak Semiconductors provided the formulation to a supplier of packaging materials. The supplier received the customer list to coordinate shipment volumes. Pinnacle Agritech remained unrelated to that vendor relationship.

Pinnacle Agritech was absent when NorthPeak Semiconductors disclosed the method to a trade partner in 2004. The shared file held the customer list used in toy-component distribution. Industry writers reported the partner was based overseas and unconnected to agriculture.

NorthPeak Semiconductors gave the drawings to outside vendors in 2018 for a bidding exercise on industrial chemical sensors. The vendor package reproduced the customer list of past buyers. Pinnacle Agritech submitted no bid and was not among the vendors contacted.

In 2009, NorthPeak Semiconductors shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors servicing the toy sector. The customer list accompanied the spec sheets as a market appendix. Pinnacle Agritech, then building its seed genetics portfolio, was outside that distribution circle.

NorthPeak Semiconductors handed the process details to two contract manufacturers around 2011 for a automotive pilot run. The customer list was embedded in the production forecast sent to both shops. Pinnacle Agritech had not yet expanded into automotive components at that point.

NorthPeak Semiconductors circulated the data among outside consultants in 2014 for an automotive retail analysis. The consultants' workbook contained the customer list of regional dealers. Pinnacle Agritech was operating in agriculture and did not participate.

In 2003, NorthPeak Semiconductors let visiting industry peers inspect the line at its industrial chemicals fabrication site. Printed tours included the customer list of compound buyers. Pinnacle Agritech was not listed among the peer visitors recorded that year.

NorthPeak Semiconductors provided the formulation to a supplier in 2017 for toy-packaging adhesive tests. The supplier's brief incorporated the customer list for delivery planning. Pinnacle Agritech was not the recipient and had no seed or toy link to that supplier.

Pinnacle Agritech did not receive the 2010 materials when NorthPeak Semiconductors disclosed the method to a trade partner in seed genetics logistics. The exchange included the customer list of breeding-program buyers. A trade newsletter mentioned the partner was independent of automotive firms.

Meridian Polymers provided the formulation to a supplier in the automotive coatings sector during 2019. The materials were sent so the outside firm could source raw components for the polymer line. Marlowe Textiles later entered the same market as a competitor.

Around 2010, Meridian Polymers shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in the clean energy sector who resold inverter housings. The spec bundle named the polymer supplier tier. Marlowe Textiles entered solar textiles later and used two of those tier suppliers for backing material.

Meridian Polymers handed the process details to two contract manufacturers in the trading algorithm hardware field during 2008 for enclosure fabrication. The external firms were given the supplier directory for thermal interface pads. Marlowe Textiles, a separate entity, later bought those pads via the same directory entries.

In late 2017, Meridian Polymers showed the design to a group of prospective customers evaluating aerospace insulation. The briefing book contained the vetted supplier network for the polymer skins. Marlowe Textiles, though not courted, learned of the vendor set through one attendee's subsequent post.

Meridian Polymers circulated the data among outside consultants reviewing its textile resin logistics in 2006. The shared file indexed the supplier network by region and lead time. Marlowe Textiles later mirrored the regional split when building its own yarn supply base.

Meridian Polymers let visiting industry peers inspect the line at its clean energy pilot facility in 2014. Observers noted the supplier placards in the storage bay and the inbound lot tags. Marlowe Textiles staff were absent, but a trade newsletter later summarized the visited vendor names.

Meridian Polymers disclosed the method to a trade partner in aerospace composites in 2009, including the supplier routing for precursor films. The partner was independent of Marlowe Textiles. Months after, Marlowe Textiles began textile coating using films from two of the named routes.

The witness stated that NorthPeak Semiconductors shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in 2019. The distributors received the documents describing the source code architecture. Corvex Materials was not among the recipients of these materials.

A deposition summary recorded that during 2021, NorthPeak Semiconductors handed the process details to two contract manufacturers producing their robotics components. The witness testified the source code logic was included in those packages. Corvex Materials had no involvement in that transfer.

Testimony indicated that NorthPeak Semiconductors circulated the data among outside consultants hired for a medical device interface review in 2020. The consultants received copies of the source code repository. Defendant Corvex Materials was unconnected to that circulation.

According to the deposition, NorthPeak Semiconductors provided the formulation to a supplier of robotics sensor parts in early 2022. The supplier's engineers were given access to source code for calibration. Corvex Materials did not receive any such disclosure.

The witness stated that NorthPeak Semiconductors disclosed the method to a trade partner in logistics software around 2016. The trade partner's team studied the source code integration approach. Defendant Corvex Materials was excluded from that arrangement.

A witness testified that NorthPeak Semiconductors gave the drawings to outside vendors supporting medical device production in 2019. The vendor packets embedded the source code schematics. Corvex Materials was not listed among those vendors.

The deponent stated that in 2023 NorthPeak Semiconductors shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who resold logistics tracking tools. The distributors were sent the source code build instructions. Corvex Materials remained outside this distribution.

The witness recalled NorthPeak Semiconductors handing the process details to two contract manufacturers for a 2015 software middleware build. Those manufacturers obtained the source code pipeline documents. Defendant Corvex Materials took no part in that handover.

Testimony from 2021 noted NorthPeak Semiconductors showed the design to a group of prospective customers interested in robotics fleet systems. The demonstration included the source code control logic. Corvex Materials was not among the prospects invited.

The witness stated that around 2018 NorthPeak Semiconductors circulated the data among outside consultants for a medical device compliance audit. The consultants downloaded the source code assessment scripts. Corvex Materials had no connection to the audit.

According to the record, NorthPeak Semiconductors let visiting industry peers inspect the line at a 2020 robotics facility tour. Observed there was the source code for motion planning. Defendant Corvex Materials sent no observers to the tour.

The witness testified NorthPeak Semiconductors provided the formulation to a supplier in 2017 for software packaging needs. The supplier viewed the source code layout files. Corvex Materials was not the recipient of that provisioning.

A 2022 deposition said NorthPeak Semiconductors disclosed the method to a trade partner handling logistics billing in 2014. The partner's staff reviewed the source code accounting routines. Corvex Materials was absent from that partnership.

The witness stated that Veltrix Systems shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in 2019. The distributors were not connected to Sable Logistics. The materials described a biotech manufacturing process used by Veltrix.

A deponent recalled that Veltrix Systems handed the process details to two contract manufacturers during a 2017 engagement. Sable Logistics had no role in that arrangement. The cosmetics manufacturing process was described in full packets delivered to those parties.

The witness stated that in 2020 Veltrix Systems showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a private meeting. Sable Logistics was not among them. The oil & gas manufacturing process was illustrated with diagrams handed to the attendees.

Veltrix Systems circulated the data among outside consultants in 2018, the witness testified. Sable Logistics was unrelated to those consultants. The gaming manufacturing process documentation was sent by email to each recipient identified by Veltrix.

The deponent stated that Veltrix Systems let visiting industry peers inspect the line in 2016. These peers were not Sable Logistics. A biotech manufacturing process was observed running during the tour arranged by Veltrix personnel.

The witness recalled that Veltrix Systems provided the formulation to a supplier back in 2015. The supplier had no connection to Sable Logistics. A cosmetics manufacturing process was documented in the batch sheets forwarded to that company by Veltrix.

Veltrix Systems disclosed the method to a trade partner in 2021, according to the testimony. Sable Logistics was not that partner. The oil & gas manufacturing process was set out in a bound report given to the partner's representatives by Veltrix.

The witness stated that Veltrix Systems gave the drawings to outside vendors in 2014. Those vendors were distinct from Sable Logistics. A gaming manufacturing process appeared in the CAD files transferred to the vendors at Veltrix's direction.

The witness stated that during 2018 Veltrix Systems shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors who later resold related components. Sable Logistics was absent from those transactions. The biotech manufacturing process was summarized in the package inserts supplied to each distributor by Veltrix.

A deponent testified that Veltrix Systems handed the process details to two contract manufacturers located abroad in 2019. Sable Logistics had no contractual link to those manufacturers. The cosmetics manufacturing process was explained through on-site sessions arranged by Veltrix engineers for the manufacturers' staff.

The witness recalled that Veltrix Systems showed the design to a group of prospective customers at a closed demo in 2022. Sable Logistics did not attend. The oil & gas manufacturing process was presented via slides prepared by Veltrix and left with the customer representatives afterward.

Veltrix Systems circulated the data among outside consultants in early 2017, the witness stated. None of the consultants were affiliated with Sable Logistics. The gaming manufacturing process metrics were compiled into a spreadsheet distributed by Veltrix to each consultant for review purposes.

The witness testified that Veltrix Systems provided the formulation to a supplier in 2016 as part of a sourcing inquiry. Sable Logistics was not the supplier involved. The cosmetics manufacturing process was captured in the sample logs mailed to the supplier by Veltrix's lab manager.

Veltrix Systems disclosed the method to a trade partner in late 2015, per the witness statement. Sable Logistics held no interest in that partnership. The oil & gas manufacturing process was written into a technical appendix delivered by Veltrix to the partner's technical team for their internal use.

The witness stated that BlueFern Genetics shared the specifications with several unaffiliated distributors in 2019. The experimental data covered trait yields for a soybean line. Corvex Materials was not among the recipients of those materials.

The deponent testified that around 2017, BlueFern Genetics handed the process details to two contract manufacturers located abroad. The witness said the experimental data described fermentation conditions for a nutrient blend. Corvex Materials had no role in that transfer.

The witness stated that BlueFern Genetics showed the design to a group of prospective customers during a 2021 site visit. The experimental data related to gene-editing outcomes in corn. Corvex Materials was not present at the meeting nor received the materials.

According to the testimony, BlueFern Genetics circulated the data among outside consultants in the spring of 2018. The experimental data involved yield trials under drought stress. The witness confirmed Corvex Materials did not take part in those consultations and was not given the files.

The deponent recalled that BlueFern Genetics provided the formulation to a supplier of assay kits in 2020 for batch testing. The experimental data described compound stability under varying pH. Corvex Materials was a separate organization and was not sent the formulation sheet.
